section.title: The Rewards of Seeking Wisdom
section.sectionRationale: The second discourse is one long, carefully built sentence in the Hebrew: if you seek wisdom, verses 1 to 4, then you will discern the fear of the LORD, verses 5 to 11, and wisdom will deliver you from two dangers, the man who speaks perversity, verses 12 to 15, and the forbidden woman, verses 16 to 19, ending in a settled inheritance for the upright, verses 20 to 22.
section.thesis: Wisdom is not stumbled upon; it is searched for like silver and hidden treasure, and to the one who seeks it, God gives discernment that protects from evil companions and the seductive path, and settles the seeker safely in the land.
section.frameNote: Four movements within one extended argument: the call to seek wisdom like treasure; the LORD's gift of wisdom that guards the seeker; deliverance from the perverse man and from the forbidden woman; and the settled inheritance of the upright contrasted with the uprooting of the wicked.

verses.text: My son, if you accept my words and hide my commandments within you,
if you incline your ear to {{chokmah|wisdom}} and direct your heart to understanding,
if you truly call out to insight and lift your voice to understanding,
if you seek it like silver and search it out like hidden treasure,
then you will discern the {{yirah|fear of the LORD}} and discover the knowledge of God.
For the LORD gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding.
He stores up sound wisdom for the upright; He is a shield to those who walk with integrity,
to guard the paths of justice and protect the way of His saints.
Then you will discern righteousness and justice and equity, every good path.
For wisdom will enter your heart, and knowledge will delight your soul.
Discretion will watch over you, and understanding will guard you,

units.label: Delivered from the perverse man and the forbidden woman

verses.text: to deliver you from the way of evil, from the man who speaks perversity,
from those who leave the straight paths to walk in the ways of darkness,
from those who enjoy doing evil and rejoice in the twistedness of evil,
whose paths are crooked and whose ways are devious.
It will rescue you from the {{zarah|forbidden woman}}, from the stranger with seductive words
who abandons the partner of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God.
For her house sinks down to death, and her tracks to the departed spirits.
None who go to her return or negotiate the paths of life.

units.label: A settled inheritance
units.note: the upright remain, the wicked are cut off

verses.text: So you will follow in the ways of the good, and keep to the paths of the righteous.
For the upright will inhabit the land, and the blameless will remain in it;
but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the unfaithful will be uprooted.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, here something to be actively sought with the same energy one would use hunting for silver or hidden treasure. It is not passively received but earnestly pursued through attentive listening and a directed heart.

yirah.gloss: The fear of the LORD, named here as the very thing wisdom seeking discovers, verse 5. It is the reverent, trusting knowledge of God that anchors and directs everything else this chapter promises, discretion, protection, and a settled inheritance.

zarah.gloss: The forbidden or strange woman, literally the foreign or estranged one, who has abandoned marriage covenant and forgotten God's covenant. In this chapter she represents the seductive path that looks like life but ends in death, a warning developed further in chapters 5 to 7.

basic.context: This whole chapter is one long sentence in the Hebrew, building a chain of promises. If you seek wisdom the way a prospector searches for silver, verses 1 to 4, then God Himself will grant you the fear of the LORD and true discernment, verses 5 to 11. That wisdom then does concrete, protective work, it rescues from two dangers that could otherwise ruin a life, the crooked man who lives to do evil, and the seductive woman who has abandoned her covenants. The result is a settled, secure life in the land, while the unfaithful are eventually uprooted.
basic.hermeneutics: The conditional structure, if you seek, then you will find, if wisdom enters, then you will be delivered, teaches that wisdom is neither automatic nor earned by human effort alone; verse 6 makes plain that the LORD Himself gives it. Human seeking and divine giving are not in competition here, the seeking is itself part of how God's gift normally comes.
basic.originalLanguages: Chokmah, wisdom, is something actively searched for like treasure, not passively absorbed. The yirah, fear of the LORD, is described as something wisdom seeking actually uncovers, verse 5, tying reverence for God to the practical discernment the whole chapter promises. And the zarah, forbidden woman, is literally the estranged or foreign one, someone who has broken her own marriage covenant and forgotten her covenant with God.
basic.typology: The picture of a way that sinks down to death and departed spirits, verse 18, anticipates the biblical theme of two ways, one leading to life and one to death, which Christ takes up directly in His teaching on the narrow and wide gates, Matthew 7:13 to 14. The settled inheritance of the upright, verse 21, foreshadows the inheritance promised to those found in Christ.
basic.christ: This chapter promises that seeking wisdom leads to the fear of the LORD, deliverance from evil, and a secure inheritance, but it also shows that wisdom must first be given by God, verse 6. The New Testament reveals the fullest gift of that wisdom in Christ, who is the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:30, and who alone can truly deliver from the crooked path and secure believers in an inheritance that cannot be uprooted, 1 Peter 1:4.
basic.god: God is generous, He gives wisdom from His own mouth, verse 6, and He is protective, a shield to those who walk with integrity, verse 7, guarding their paths like a watchman. He is also just, so that in the end the wicked, who abandon His covenant, are cut off, while the faithful remain secure.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 7:13 to 14 speaks of two ways, echoing this chapter's two paths of life and death. 1 Corinthians 1:30 calls Christ our wisdom from God. James 1:5 promises wisdom to those who ask. 1 Peter 1:4 describes an inheritance kept in heaven, imperishable and unfading.
basic.oneStory: From early in Proverbs, the pursuit of wisdom is tied to rescue from destructive paths and to a settled, secure future. That pattern, seek and be delivered, points forward to the gospel's deeper rescue, in which Christ, the wisdom of God, delivers those who seek Him from sin's crooked path and secures them in an inheritance that can never be uprooted.

context.literary:
Proverbs 2 is built with unusual care, and the care shows the argument. It has twenty two verses, the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, though it is not an acrostic, and many readers hear a quiet signal of completeness, wisdom from A to Z. Its grammar is a single chain. Verses 1 to 4 are a set of conditions, each opening with 'if'. Verses 5 and 9 each begin a 'then'. Verses 12 and 16 both open with an infinitive that means 'to deliver you,' once from the way of evil and once from the forbidden woman. Verse 20 opens a final purpose clause, 'so you will follow in the ways of the good,' and verses 21 and 22 give the grounds. The whole poem is one long thought.

The verse counts fall into a pattern, four, four, three, four, four, three. Verses 1 to 4 are the learner's part, verses 5 to 8 are God's part, verses 9 to 11 describe wisdom entering the heart, verses 12 to 15 deliver from the perverse man, verses 16 to 19 from the forbidden woman, and verses 20 to 22 close with the road and the land. The poem has two halves: what you must do, and what that will do for you.

The first four verses pile up eight verbs, two to a verse, that describe seeking with the whole body: accept, treasure, incline the ear, direct the heart, call out, lift the voice, seek, search. Ear, heart and voice are all engaged, so wisdom is something one hears, desires and asks for at once.

The two dangers in the middle are matched in form. The perverse man and the forbidden woman each receive a description of their ways and a statement of where they lead, and each comes under the same verb of rescue. They are the two typical seductions of the young, violence and crooked speech on the one side and betrayal in love on the other, and chapter 2 prepares for the long warnings about them in chapters 5 to 7. It also follows chapter 1, where the gang enticed and Wisdom called in the street; here the father shows what receiving that call will do.
context.historical:
The images of the opening verses come from the world of the miner. Job 28:1-11 describes how people probe the farthest recesses for silver and gold, cutting shafts in places forgotten by the foot of man, and then asks the question that Proverbs 2 answers, where wisdom is found. To an Israelite who knew that silver was dug from deep in the ground at great cost and risk, to be told to seek wisdom 'like silver' and 'like hidden treasure' was a demand for the same ferocity of effort. Jesus' parable of treasure hidden in a field is in the same tradition, Matthew 13:44.

The repeated promise to 'inhabit the land,' verse 21, is covenant language. Moses told Israel to keep the statutes so that they might live and enter and take possession of the land, Deuteronomy 4:1, and warned that the faithless would be uprooted from it, Deuteronomy 28:63. For a family in ancient Israel the land was the visible sign of belonging, and losing it was the shape of disaster. A sage who ends a poem on staying in the land, or being cut off from it, was speaking in the strongest terms that his hearers knew. After the exile those words would have weighed even more.

The forbidden woman, a phrase that literally means a strange or estranged woman, belongs to a world where marriage was covenant, not merely contract. Malachi calls the wife of one's youth a companion and a wife by covenant, with the LORD as witness, Malachi 2:14. In verse 17 she forgets 'the covenant of her God,' and the word for her husband, the partner of her youth, is one that Jeremiah 3:4 uses of God Himself as 'my friend from youth.' Israel had also met the seduction of foreign cults and foreign women, at Baal of Peor, Numbers 25:1-3, and in the later life of Solomon, whose foreign wives turned his heart away, 1 Kings 11:1-4.

The 'departed spirits' of verse 18 are the Rephaim, the shades of the dead in the ancient picture of Sheol, which Psalm 88:10 and Isaiah 14:9 mention. In that world death was a place of shadows, and the sage uses it to say that this road has one end.
context.canonical:
The first four verses stand in a line of Scripture that promises that seekers will find. Moses told Israel in exile that they would find the LORD if they sought Him with all their heart and soul, Deuteronomy 4:29, and Jeremiah repeats it, 'You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart,' Jeremiah 29:13. Wisdom herself says in Proverbs 8:17 that those who seek her early find her, and Proverbs 8:10-11 asks for instruction in place of silver. Jesus gathers it into a promise, 'Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you,' Matthew 7:7-8. Proverbs 2 is the sage's version of that invitation.

Verse 6 is the doctrine behind it. The LORD gives wisdom, and the New Testament takes the same line: 'if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all,' James 1:5, and Paul prays that God may give a spirit of wisdom and revelation, Ephesians 1:17. Behind it too is the promise of the new covenant that God would put His law in minds and inscribe it on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33, so that wisdom entering the heart, as in verse 10, is the pattern of what God finally does for His people.

The forbidden woman is part of a series. She appears again in Proverbs 5:3-6, where her lips drip honey and her steps lead to Sheol, in Proverbs 7, and at last in Proverbs 9:13-18 as Folly, the rival of Wisdom. The prophets use the imagery of unfaithfulness for Israel's idolatry, which gives the picture a larger frame, and Revelation takes it up in the great prostitute who corrupted the earth, Revelation 17:1-5.

The promise of the land is carried into the New Testament and enlarged. The Psalms tell the meek and the righteous that they will inherit the land, Psalm 37:9-11, and Jesus says that the meek will inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5. Paul says that the promise to Abraham was that he would be heir of the world, Romans 4:13, and Peter speaks of an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, 1 Peter 1:4.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The father is teaching his son to want wisdom. The poem does not begin by describing wisdom but by describing the posture of a person who really seeks it, and the verbs get more urgent with each line. A passive son who is told the right answers is not what he wants. He wants a son who goes after wisdom with the energy of a prospector and who treats it as the most valuable thing he could possess.

He also means to make clear that wisdom is not a technique for getting ahead. The fruit of seeking is the fear of the LORD and the knowledge of God, verse 5, and a recognition of righteousness, justice and equity, every good path, verse 9. Wisdom here is moral and relational before it is practical. The reward is not a clever mind but a protected life, and the protection is real: the two figures from whom wisdom delivers are both people who would destroy the son through his own desires.

The poem is also written to let the son see that his own effort is held inside God's gift. Verses 1 to 4 describe what the son must do, verses 5 to 8 describe what the LORD does, and the 'then' of verse 5 depends on both. The father does not want pride in the son's achievement or despair at his weakness. He wants him to look to the LORD, who stores up sound wisdom for the upright.

Finally, the closing verses are for those who might drift. The land is for the blameless and the uprooting is for the unfaithful, so a son who is tempted to think that crookedness gets away with it is shown where each road ends.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The 'if' and 'then' construction is a prescription for how to seek and a description of what usually follows, and the two should not be confused with a contract. The chapter does not promise that the seeker will be rich or free from trouble. The promises are of wisdom, the knowledge of God, protection from two specific kinds of ruin and a settled place among the faithful. Other sayings and other books remind the reader that the righteous sometimes suffer for years, as Psalm 37 acknowledges, and the reward is the shape of a life lived with God, which is not always visible at every stage.

The warnings about the forbidden woman need a similar care. They are addressed to a son in a male voice, and the pattern is meant to fit any person facing seduction, so that a woman reading this should hear the same call to refuse the person who betrays covenant. 'None who go to her return,' verse 19, states how seldom and how hardly a person comes back from that road, not that God's forgiveness is impossible. David was forgiven after adultery, 2 Samuel 12:13, and Jesus told a woman caught in adultery that He did not condemn her, and also told her to go and sin no more, John 8:11. The proverb warns so that no one will have to learn the lesson the hard way.

What carries over directly is the posture. Believers are to treasure God's words, to ask Him for wisdom and to flee what would ruin them, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 6:18, with the confidence that the God who commands also protects.

debates.question: Is wisdom something the seeker earns or something God gives?

views.label: It comes through diligent human effort
views.case: Verses 1 to 4 are full of effort: accept, treasure, call, seek, search. The illustration of a miner makes wisdom sound hard won, and Proverbs 8:17 says those who seek early find. On this reading the sage is urging disciplined study and practice, with wisdom as the reward.

views.label: It is entirely God's gift
views.case: Verse 6 says, 'the LORD gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding,' and James 1:5 tells those who lack wisdom to ask. Paul says that Christ became wisdom for us, 1 Corinthians 1:30. On this reading the seeking is itself a response that God makes possible.

views.label: Both are true and belong together
views.case: The text sets them side by side without a seam. The 'if' clauses are the seeker's part and verses 5 to 8 are God's, and Jesus joins them in the call to ask, seek and knock, Matthew 7:7-8, with the promise that the door is opened and the gift is given. Proverbs 3:5-6 pairs trusting the LORD with all one's heart with acknowledging Him in all one's ways.

debates.bearing: The third view fits the text best. Seeking is the way God ordinarily gives wisdom, and the one who has received it does not boast, since it was given from His mouth.

debates.question: Who is the 'forbidden woman' of verse 16?

views.label: A literal adulteress, a married woman who seduces the young
views.case: Proverbs 7 describes her in a narrative: her husband has gone on a long journey, and she lures a young man, Proverbs 7:19-20. Verse 17 says she has left the partner of her youth, which is language of marriage. The warning is plain moral instruction about adultery.

views.label: A foreign woman, with the danger of idolatry in view
views.case: The word translated stranger or foreign is also used of non Israelite women, and the verse speaks of forgetting the covenant of her God. Israel's history is full of the danger, Numbers 25:1-3 and 1 Kings 11:1-4, where sexual and religious unfaithfulness went together.

views.label: A figure for Folly, the rival of Wisdom, who stands for every seductive alternative
views.case: Proverbs 9:13-18 sets the woman called Folly against Lady Wisdom, using the same invitation, and the prophets treat Israel's idolatry as adultery. On this reading the figure is real and also larger, a picture of any offer that betrays covenant loyalty for pleasure.

debates.bearing: These readings are not exclusive. The literal danger is real, and the poet knew that it carries a larger meaning. Any of them leads to the same practice, which is to refuse the voice that offers pleasure at the cost of covenant faithfulness.

debates.question: What does 'inhabit the land' mean for the reader now, verse 21?

views.label: The land of Israel, as a covenant promise to that people
views.case: The language of staying in and being cut off from the land is the covenant language of Deuteronomy, Deuteronomy 4:1 and 28:63. In its first setting the promise was to Israel in Canaan, and the exile showed what being uprooted meant.

views.label: A general pattern of settled life for the righteous
views.case: Proverbs 10:30 says that the righteous will never be shaken but the wicked will not inhabit the land, in the form of a general proverb. Read as wisdom, it says that faithful living tends toward stability and unfaithfulness toward upheaval.

views.label: A promise that widens to the inheritance of the whole earth and the age to come
views.case: Psalm 37:29 says the righteous will inherit the land and dwell in it forever, Jesus says the meek will inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5, and Hebrews says the patriarchs were longing for a better country, a heavenly one, Hebrews 11:16. On this reading the land is an early form of a larger inheritance.

debates.bearing: The Bible's own movement suggests that the second and third readings grow out of the first. A Christian reader takes the promise as a pattern of life and as the hope of the world to come, without reading it as a guarantee of comfortable circumstances.

study.originalLanguages:
Two verbs in the chapter share a root that the English hides. In verse 1 the son is to 'hide' my commandments within him, and in verse 7 the LORD 'stores up' sound wisdom for the upright. Both are the verb tsaphan, to treasure up or to store. Psalm 31:19 uses it for the goodness God has laid up for those who fear Him, and Psalm 119:11 for the word hidden in the heart. The son treasures God's words and God treasures wisdom for the son. They meet in the same safe place, and the exchange is the argument of the chapter in two verbs.

The word for sound wisdom in verse 7, tushiyyah, carries the idea of something solid and effective, wisdom that works and lasts, and it is something the LORD keeps in store, so the upright are drawing on a supply that does not run out. The upright, yesharim, belongs to a root for straight, the opposite of the crooked paths of verses 13 and 15. The same root gives the word 'equity' in verse 9, meisharim, so wisdom's goal and the wise person's character are both said to be straightness.

The two dangers are described with the same family of words. The man who speaks 'perversity' in verse 12, tahpukhot, is literally the speech of turning things upside down, from the verb to overturn, and verse 14 says that such people rejoice in the 'twistedness' of evil, the same noun. This is a picture of an inversion of values, calling evil good, a danger the prophets warned against in Isaiah 5:20. The picture of the paths is also pointed: wisdom walks the straight and level road, and these men are on a crooked one.

The forbidden woman in verse 16 is zarah, the strange one, and the poet pairs her with nokhriyyah, the foreign or alien one, so that she is a person who has become a stranger to her own commitments. Verse 17 calls her husband alluf, a word for a close companion that elsewhere can name a guide or chief. Jeremiah 3:4 uses it of God, 'my friend from youth,' so the woman who abandons the alluf of her youth is doing what Israel did to the LORD. The 'covenant of her God' is the marriage vow as a thing made before God, with Malachi 2:14 as the commentary, or perhaps the covenant of Sinai, and the verse leaves both in view.

Verse 18 speaks of 'departed spirits,' rephaim, the shades of the dead, which Psalm 88:10 and Isaiah 14:9 mention. Verse 19 says none who go to her 'return,' from the verb shuv that also means to turn back or repent, so the road is so downhill that turning back is hard. In verse 22 the wicked will be 'uprooted,' yissachu, from the verb nasach, which Deuteronomy 28:63 uses for being uprooted from the land, and 'cut off,' yikkaretu, from karat, which is also the verb for cutting a covenant. Those who broke covenant are cut from it.

Finally the word for knowledge in verse 5, da'at, appears with 'of God,' the knowledge of God, which Hosea 4:1 says has gone missing in the land. The seeker's reward is not only information but acquaintance with God Himself.

typology.type: Seeking wisdom like hidden treasure, verses 3 to 4
typology.fulfillment: The father tells his son to search for wisdom as a miner searches for silver and treasure, and Jesus gives the same shape to the kingdom: the kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man finds and, in his joy, sells all he has to buy, Matthew 13:44. The pearl merchant does the same, Matthew 13:45-46. Colossians says that in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Colossians 2:3. The escalation is that the treasure is a person, and its worth exceeds everything sold to gain it. The type is limited because the sage's miner discovers by effort, while the man in the field is surprised by joy and the gift of Christ is not earned by digging.

typology.type: The LORD as shield and guard of the faithful, verses 7 to 8
typology.fulfillment: The LORD is a shield to those who walk with integrity and guards the way of His saints. The pattern first appears in God's word to Abram, 'I am your shield, your very great reward,' Genesis 15:1, and the psalmist says He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him, Psalm 18:30. In the Gospel of John, Jesus says that no one can snatch His sheep from His hand, John 10:28, and prays that He has protected and preserved those the Father gave Him, John 17:12. The shield of the old covenant becomes the Shepherd who holds His people. The correspondence is still partial: the shield protects in the way of the faithful, while Christ also dies in place of the unfaithful, the very ones who need protection from themselves.

typology.type: The faithless wife and the faithful Bridegroom, verses 16 to 17
typology.fulfillment: The forbidden woman forgets the covenant of her God and abandons the partner of her youth. The prophets use the same figure of Israel, and in Hosea God declares, 'I will betroth you to Me forever, I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion,' Hosea 2:19-20. In the New Testament the church is the bride whom Christ loved and gave Himself up for, to present her holy and blameless, Ephesians 5:25-27, and the great prostitute of Revelation 17:1-5 is the final form of the seduction the father warned against. The type is only an echo here: Proverbs 2 speaks of one woman and one son, and the larger story of the bride is the work of later Scripture.

typology.type: The paths of life against the way that sinks to death, verses 18 to 20
typology.fulfillment: The chapter sets two roads, the paths of the good and a house that sinks down to death. Jesus takes up the same picture in His teaching about the narrow gate that leads to life and the wide gate and broad road that lead to destruction, Matthew 7:13-14. Peter, preaching at Pentecost, quotes David, 'You have made known to me the paths of life,' and says that this was spoken of the resurrection of Christ, Acts 2:25-28. The escalation is that the path of life now runs through an empty tomb and that Jesus is Himself the way, John 14:6. The proverb's picture is still in force, but the path to life is now more than moral wisdom, it is a person who has already gone through death and out the other side.

study.christ:
Proverbs 2 never names the Messiah, and the honest way to read it as pointing to Christ is to follow the paths that the New Testament itself draws.

The central link is the question that verse 6 raises: where does wisdom come from, and who can give it? The answer is 'the LORD gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding.' Paul looks at the person of Jesus and says that He has become for us wisdom from God, our righteousness, holiness and redemption, 1 Corinthians 1:30, and that in Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Colossians 2:3. The seeker who is told to look for wisdom like hidden treasure finds that the treasure has a face. Jesus Himself says that the kingdom is a treasure for which a man gladly sells all, Matthew 13:44, and He promises that the one who seeks will find, Matthew 7:7-8.

The second link is the protection of verses 7 to 11. The LORD is a shield to those who walk with integrity, and discretion and understanding will guard the one in whom wisdom has taken root. Jesus says of those the Father has given Him that no one can snatch them from His hand, John 10:28, and in prayer that He protected and preserved them, John 17:12. The guard of the faithful is not left to their own prudence; it is the Shepherd's hand.

The third link concerns the forbidden woman and the faithless partner. The covenant of marriage in Proverbs is a picture that the prophets and apostles enlarge. Hosea hears God promise to betroth His people forever in righteousness, justice, loving devotion and compassion, Hosea 2:19-20, and Paul says that Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her, to present her to Himself holy and blameless, Ephesians 5:25-27. The One who is the faithful Bridegroom is also the Saviour of those who have been unfaithful. The woman caught in adultery is told by Jesus that He does not condemn her, John 8:11, and so even those who have walked the road that sinks down to death are not beyond the reach of the One who came to save them.

The fourth link is the two roads. Jesus teaches that the narrow gate leads to life and the wide gate to destruction, Matthew 7:13-14, and Peter applies David's words, 'You have made known to me the paths of life,' to the resurrection of Christ, Acts 2:25-28. The proverb says the wicked will be cut off and the upright remain, and the New Testament tells us that Christ is the upright One who was cut off on behalf of the unrighteous and who now holds the inheritance, which is kept for His people, 1 Peter 1:4 and Hebrews 9:15.

A caution is needed. The chapter does not say that the silver is Jesus or that the woman is the devil. What it gives is the pattern that Christ fulfils: wisdom given from God's mouth, protection by His hand, and a settled inheritance for those who stay with Him.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the giver and not merely the object of the search. Verse 6 is the hinge of the poem. The seeker has been told to call and search, and now he learns that what he seeks is already offered by the One who speaks. 'From His mouth come knowledge and understanding' makes wisdom the product of God's speech, as the whole creation was, and so the one who listens for wisdom is listening for God. That is why James can say that God gives generously to all without finding fault, James 1:5. God is not grudging with what He gives, and He does not shame the one who asks.

He is also a keeper and treasurer. Verse 7 says He 'stores up' sound wisdom, the same verb used for the seeker's treasuring in verse 1, and Psalm 31:19 says that He has laid up goodness for those who fear Him. The picture is of a God who has prepared good things ahead of the seeker's arrival and whose supply is large enough for everyone who comes.

He is a shield and a guard. The poem uses two verbs of protection, to guard the paths of justice and to protect the way of His saints, verse 8, and then says wisdom and discretion will keep watch over the seeker, verse 11. Genesis 15:1 gives the first word, 'I am your shield,' and Psalm 1:6 says the LORD guards the path of the righteous. The God of Proverbs 2 protects by giving wisdom that spots danger, so that protection comes through the formation of the person and not only through rescue from outside.

He is the God of the covenant at home. The 'covenant of her God' in verse 17 means that He is a party to the marriage vow, and Malachi 2:14 says the LORD is a witness between a man and the wife of his youth. God cares about faithfulness in the most private bonds of life, and a breach of them is a breach against Him.

He is just, and His justice settles accounts. The way of the wicked leads to death and they are cut off from the land and uprooted, verses 18 and 22. Yet the justice is not arbitrary: the upright remain, and the wicked reap what they have chosen. The God of this chapter is neither indifferent to evil nor eager to punish. He lays out two ways clearly and tells the son which one leads to life.

He is, finally, a God to be known. The chapter's goal is 'the knowledge of God,' verse 5, and Hosea shows what it is to lose it in a land. For worship, the poem asks us to seek God with the whole body, ear, heart and voice, and to give thanks that He has already put the treasure within reach.

crossReferences.note: Miners probe the farthest recesses for silver and gold, cutting shafts in places no foot has been. Job uses this to ask where wisdom is found, and Proverbs 2:4 picks up the same image to say that wisdom deserves the miner's whole effort.

Moses promises that if Israel seeks the LORD with all its heart and soul it will find Him. It is the covenant root of the 'if you seek' of verses 3 and 4, and shows that seeking wisdom is a form of seeking God.

God tells the exiles that they will seek Him and find Him when they search with all their heart. It repeats the promise of Proverbs 2:3 to 5 to a people who had lost the land, and it gives the same pairing of earnest effort and sure reward.

Jesus says, 'Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened.' It takes the sage's call to seek and turns it into a promise made by the one who holds the answer.

The psalmist rejoices in the goodness God has laid up for those who fear Him. The verb is the same as in Proverbs 2:7, where the LORD stores up sound wisdom for the upright, so both texts show a God who provides in advance.
God tells Abram, 'I am your shield, your very great reward.' It is the first time God is called a shield in Scripture and underlies 'He is a shield to those who walk with integrity' in Proverbs 2:7.

The lips of the forbidden woman drip honey, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, and her steps lead straight to Sheol. It expands the warning of 2:16 to 19 and gives the same destination, so the father's promise of deliverance rests on a clear account of the danger.

Folly sits at her door and calls the simple to her house, where her guests are in the depths of Sheol. It shows that the forbidden woman of chapter 2 has a larger meaning, the rival of Wisdom, and brings the two-house contrast of the whole section to a close.

The LORD has been a witness between a man and the wife of his youth, who is his companion and wife by covenant. It explains the phrase 'the covenant of her God' in 2:17 and shows that marriage is a vow made before Him.

God promises to betroth His people to Himself forever in righteousness, justice, loving devotion and compassion. It sets a faithful divine husband against the faithless partner of Proverbs 2:17 and widens the picture from one marriage to the covenant itself.

The righteous will inherit the land and dwell in it forever. It repeats the promise of Proverbs 2:21 with the addition of 'forever,' so that the settled life of the upright is heard as an abiding inheritance.

Jesus tells His hearers to enter by the narrow gate, for the wide gate and broad road lead to destruction and the small gate and narrow way lead to life. It is the two-way teaching of Proverbs 2:12 to 22 made into a decision at the door.

Christ Jesus has become for us wisdom from God, our righteousness, holiness and redemption. It answers the question of Proverbs 2:6, who gives wisdom, with a person, and shows that what the seeker is promised is received through Him.

Peter says the new birth in Christ brings an inheritance kept in heaven that cannot spoil or fade. It carries the promise of settled possession in Proverbs 2:21 to a certainty that no exile, invasion or death can uproot, because the One who guards it is God.

study.oneStory:
The first story of the Bible is about the wrong way to seek wisdom. The woman saw that the tree was 'desirable for obtaining wisdom,' Genesis 3:6, and took it by her own hand, and what she got was the exposure of her nakedness and the loss of the garden. Proverbs 2 is a counter story. The wisdom that cannot be taken can be received, and the one who asks of the LORD, who stores it up for the upright, is given it from His mouth. The garden gave a lesson in what happens when seeking is a grab. This chapter teaches what seeking looks like when it is trust.

The land is the other great thread. God promised Abraham a land, brought Israel into a place full of houses they had not built, and warned them not to forget Him in their prosperity, Deuteronomy 6:10-12. The promise was conditional on faithfulness, and the history of Israel shows what happened to those who were unfaithful, those who broke the covenant of their God and were uprooted. The father's closing verses are a miniature of Deuteronomy 28. Behind the warning is the experience of exile, and behind the exile is the fall from the garden. The story keeps going east, away from the presence of God, until the whole structure of seeking and inheriting is made new.

The forbidden woman has her place in that story too. The prophets use her picture for Israel, who forgot her covenant, and Hosea hears God say that He will betroth her again, Hosea 2:19-20. The New Testament speaks of the church as a bride prepared for her Husband, Revelation 21:2, and the great prostitute of Revelation 17 stands as the final seduction. The warnings of the father are a small piece of a very large conflict.

In Christ the story turns. The treasure of wisdom is found in Him, Colossians 2:3, and He gives His people the protection that Proverbs describes, John 10:28. The inheritance that the upright were to hold in the land becomes an inheritance that cannot perish or fade, 1 Peter 1:4, which Christ obtained as mediator of a new covenant, Hebrews 9:15.

The story ends in a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells, 2 Peter 3:13, and where the one who overcomes will inherit all things, Revelation 21:7. The meek inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5, and God's people will see His face, Revelation 22:4. The paths that wisdom once guarded become a single road into the city of God, and the knowledge of the LORD that the father taught his son to seek is known fully at last, 1 Corinthians 13:12.

quiz.q: According to verses 1 to 4, how is wisdom meant to be pursued?

options.text: Earnestly, like searching for silver or hidden treasure.
options.note: Verse 4 gives this exact image of vigorous, determined seeking.

options.text: Passively, waiting for it to arrive without effort.
options.note: The passage is full of active verbs, accept, hide, incline, call, seek, search.

options.text: Only through formal schooling.
options.note: The passage speaks of the heart and the will, not a specific institution.

options.text: By reading widely, without any particular urgency.
options.note: Reading and listening matter, verse 2, but the passage's emphasis is on urgent, treasure hunting intensity, not casual reading.

quiz.q: What does verse 5 say seeking wisdom leads to discovering?

options.text: The fear of the LORD and the knowledge of God.
options.note: This is stated directly and is the pivot of the whole chapter's argument.

options.text: Financial prosperity alone.
options.note: The passage's emphasis is relational and moral, knowing God, not merely material gain.

options.text: Political influence.
options.note: Not the subject of this passage at all.

options.text: A general sense of self confidence.
options.note: Confidence may follow, but the text is specific, it names the fear of the LORD and knowledge of God, not vague self assurance.

quiz.q: From what two dangers does wisdom deliver, according to verses 12 to 19?

options.text: The man who speaks perversity and the forbidden woman who has broken her covenants.
options.note: These are named explicitly as the two dangers wisdom rescues from.

options.text: Poverty and old age.
options.note: These are not the dangers named in this passage.

options.text: Foreign armies and famine.
options.note: The passage's dangers are moral and relational, not military or agricultural.

options.text: Laziness and gossip only.
options.note: These are real concerns elsewhere in Proverbs but are not the specific dangers named in this chapter.

quiz.q: What is the outcome for the upright versus the wicked, verses 21 to 22?

options.text: The upright inhabit the land securely, while the wicked and unfaithful are cut off and uprooted.
options.note: This is the exact closing contrast of the chapter.

options.text: Both groups end up in the same condition eventually.
options.note: The passage draws a sharp, deliberate contrast between the two outcomes.

options.text: The wicked prosper while the upright struggle.
options.note: This reverses the passage's actual claim.

options.text: The outcome depends entirely on outward wealth.
options.note: The passage's contrast is about moral standing and security, not wealth as such.

quiz.q: How does this chapter's promise of a settled inheritance relate to Christ?

options.text: It anticipates the imperishable inheritance kept in heaven for those found in Christ.
options.note: 1 Peter 1:4 describes exactly this kind of secure, unshakable inheritance.

options.text: It has no connection to New Testament promises.
options.note: The New Testament directly echoes this language of a kept, secure inheritance.

options.text: It means every believer will own physical land.
options.note: This flattens the promise into a literal reading the New Testament expands into a greater, spiritual inheritance.

options.text: It refers only to ancient Israel's possession of Canaan, with no wider meaning.
options.note: That original reference is real, but the New Testament draws out a fuller, ongoing fulfillment in the inheritance kept for believers in Christ.

questions: Verse 4 pictures seeking wisdom like searching for hidden treasure. How much energy and priority are you actually giving to seeking wisdom from God's word right now?

The chapter says wisdom guards against the man who speaks perversity and the woman who abandons her covenants. What relationships or voices in your life pull you away from faithfulness, whether to God or to the people you have committed to?
Verse 17 describes the forbidden woman as one who has forgotten the covenant of her God. Where might you be drifting from a commitment you once made, whether to God, a spouse, or a community?
The chapter promises a settled, secure inheritance for the upright. What would it look like to trust God's security instead of scrambling to secure your own future through compromise?

Christ is called the wisdom of God, sought and given just as this chapter describes. What is one area of your life where you need to actively seek Him for wisdom this week, rather than relying only on your own judgment?

translationNotes.note: Forbidden woman can also be rendered wayward wife or adulteress; the Hebrew word itself means stranger or foreign one, pointing to estrangement from covenant faithfulness.

The departed spirits renders a Hebrew word literally meaning the Rephaim, a term for the shades of the dead, underscoring that the forbidden path leads, quite literally in the poetry, to the realm of death.
